\begin{theorem}\label{night:P3F.10}
\StatementRecord{night:P3F.10}{proved}{}{\cref{night:P3F.6}, \cref{night:P3F.9}, \cref{iv:correction:P3K.6}, \cref{night:P3K.9}}
\par\noindent\textit{Dependency scope.} We use \cref{iv:correction:P3K.6} only at their stated retained-construction or corrected-conclusion scopes.


Retain the original sphere twists \((0,1,-1)\), the reference cusp fan, the marked \(\gamma\)-circle and stable boundary comparison of \cref{night:P3F.9}. Choose the regular binding over \(t_*\notin\{0,1,\infty\}\), with the physical circle line \(M=\mathcal O(P-O)\). The resulting page has twelve positive nodal fibres and boundary \(T^3\). Its circle-line square is \(s_\delta=-2\), and its relative Pontryagin pairing in this boundary framing is \(p_{\rm rel}=-24\).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item Here the data are the original sphere twists \((0,1,-1)\). On the ordinary and finite-cap orbit pieces, use the invariant \(\gamma\) character in smooth flat coordinates. The resulting three-dimensional quotient is formed from \(S^1_\gamma\) times the punctured base and the two solid tori

\[
(S^1_\gamma\times\Delta_s)/\bigl\langle(g,s)\longmapsto(g+\ell_j/m_j,\zeta_js)\bigr\rangle.
\]

\item The two meridian relations are \(3x=\gamma\) and \(4y=-\gamma\); after the cusp solid torus the third is \(x+y=0\). The relation matrix, in the displayed row order and columns \((x,y,\gamma)\), is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&0&-1\\0&4&1\\1&1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), with determinant \(-3+4=1\). The union of the two Seifert solid tori is explicitly the standard weighted circle fibration on \(S^3\) with weights \(3,4\). Its meridian/longitude basis change is unimodular, and the two stabilizer orders are \(3,4\). This supplies the Seifert identification, including the labelled exceptional fibres.

\item To compare the smooth flat coordinates with the holomorphic logarithmic gluing, subtract the angular translation from \((\log s)/(2\pi i)\,\Pi v_j\). The remaining radial translation is single valued on the annulus and has a real scalar homotopy to zero. Translation by this homotopy on a collar gives the required equivariant identification. At the cusp use P3F.9, relative to the outer \(\gamma\) marking. This constructs a smooth map of the actual orbit \(Y=S^5\) to the weighted \(S^3\). Its fibres are the source elliptic curves; the critical curve is the nodal critical point in \(E_{I_1}\times S^1_\gamma\). Near that curve its formula is the ordinary positive node map \((x,y,\gamma)\longmapsto(xy,\gamma)\). Thus it is an actual one-parameter family of positive genus-one Lefschetz maps. The cusp modification is included in the construction of this map.

\item Choose as binding a regular weighted fibre at a value \(t_*\notin\{0,1,\infty\}\). Its Milnor open-book page is explicitly the affine curve \(b^3-a^4=1\), embedded in \(S^3\) by

\[
(a,b)\longmapsto(\rho^3a,\rho^4b),\qquad
\rho^6|a|^2+\rho^8|b|^2=1,\quad\rho>0.
\]

\item The inverse divides by the positive twelfth root of \(b^3-a^4\) on the chosen argument page. Its projection to the weighted base is the degree-12 map of P3F.6, followed by the unique Möbius map sending the binding value to \(t_*\). After adding the boundary circle the page is a genus-three surface \(C^\circ\) with one boundary component. The regular cusp fibre in the weighted \(S^3\) intersects this page in twelve points. Their signs are positive in the complex Milnor orientation, equivalently the map to the base is holomorphic and unramified there. Its inverse image \(V_0\) in \(Y\) is therefore a genus-one Lefschetz fibration over \(C^\circ\) with twelve positive nodal fibres. The boundary is the torus mapping torus of a translation, hence \(T^3\). It need not be \(S^3\).

\item The page can be chosen disjoint from the fixed sphere: by P3F.9 its \(\gamma\) image lies in an arbitrarily short arc, and the phase of the Milnor page can be chosen so that its twelve intersections with the critical \(\gamma\) circle avoid that arc. The \(\delta\)-circle bundle therefore restricts to an honest principal circle bundle over \(V_0\).

\item We justify the comparison with its sectioned Jacobian without requiring a section of a compact torsor. The affine elliptic bundle over \(C^\circ\) is locally the stated Jacobian, including the irreducible nodal fibres. Its torsor obstruction lies in \(H^2(C^\circ,j_*\Lambda_E)\). This group is zero: cut the surface along its handle generators and disjoint paths to the nodal values. In the punctured surface fundamental group, every nodal meridian is an independent free generator because the boundary word is not imposed as a relation. The restriction map from cocycles to the direct sum of their cusp coinvariants is consequently surjective. The exact sequence for \(j_*\Lambda_E\) gives \(H^2=0\). Equivalently this is the integer \v{C}ech obstruction to matching the local origins. The sheaf of smooth Lie-algebra sections is fine, so this vanishing constructs a smooth global section and an affine identification with the Jacobian.

\item The circle line has the fibrewise Picard class of \(P\), not \(6P\). This follows both from the source definition \(M=\mathcal O(P-O)\) and from its two elliptic period multipliers: the \(u\) column contains \(\mu\) while the \(\gamma\) column contains \(6\mu\). The latter records translation in the suspension. Under an affine identification of a torus torsor with its Jacobian, a degree zero line has the same Picard point. The quotient of two lines with the same normalized fibrewise Picard point is pulled back from the base: normalize a trivializing holomorphic fibre section at the chosen origin, and its overlap ratios are constant on the compact fibres. This argument remains valid at each irreducible node, where the multiplicative gluing unit is the one supplied by \(M\) and a local ball has no line-bundle obstruction. Thus on \(V_0\) its Chern class is that of the Jacobian line \(\mathcal O(P'-O')\), up to a base pullback. Since the base has boundary, that pullback is topologically trivial.

\item On the boundary regular torus the degree-zero line has unitary flat fibre multipliers and the translating point has a flat lift. Thus its restriction to \(T^3\) has zero Chern class. A relative lift of its Chern class exists. If \(u\) and \(u+\delta g\) are two lifts, with \(g\in H^1(\partial V_0;\mathbb Z)\), the absolute class of \(\delta g\) is zero and the restriction of the absolute class of \(u\) to the boundary is zero. The relative cup-product boundary formula gives

\[
u\smile\delta g=\delta(i^*u\smile g)=0,\qquad(\delta g)^2=0.
\]

\item The relative square is therefore independent of every boundary gauge. Choose the affine boundary identification furnished by the section above and cap the Jacobian by its regular fibre times \(D^2\). This gives the compact elliptic pullback under the regular-binding cover of P3F.6, with twelve \(I_1\) fibres. Its \(P'-O'\) line extends the actual page line with some boundary gauge; gauge independence now makes

\[
s_\delta=(P'-O')^2=-2\chi-2(P'\cdot O')=-2.
\]

\item This is the square of the section line \(P\), not the square of \(6P\). The proof uses a section only on the surface with boundary; it does not make any claim about a section on a compact genus-one torsor.

\item The same affine comparison identifies the relative stable tangent framing with the regular product cap framing up to a map with zero Pontryagin winding. Indeed its derivative is triangular with identity linear derivative on the elliptic translation directions. The remaining diagonal factors are complex line scalings; their maps factor through a product of \(U(1)\) groups. The universal degree-three Pontryagin transgression vanishes on that torus (equivalently each line factor has zero \(\pi_3\)), even when those scalings depend on all boundary variables. The triangular part is contracted by scaling its off-diagonal block. The regular product cap has zero relative contribution. Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
\chi(\mathcal O_{\text{capped Jacobian}})&=1,\\
\operatorname{signature}(V_0)&=\operatorname{signature}(\text{capped Jacobian})=-8,\\
p_{\rm rel}&=\int_{\text{capped Jacobian}}p_1=3\operatorname{signature}=-24.
\end{aligned}
\]

\item The signature equality uses the regular fibre neighbourhood \(T^2\times D^2\), whose intersection form has zero signature; gluing along the closed \(T^3\) boundary gives additivity. These statements give the page and its actual line and framing data. The required actual return comparison is the real spin bordism P3K.6--7, and its normal-frame term is computed in P3K.9. Thus the later finite-group conclusion uses both the page calculation and that geometric comparison.

\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{night:P3F.11}
\StatementRecord{night:P3F.11}{proved}{}{\cref{night:P3F.3}, \cref{night:P3F.4}, \cref{night:P3F.7}, \cref{night:P3F.8}, \cref{night:P3K.7}; \cite[Theorem A, p.~621]{Smale1959E}; \cite[Theorem 4.9, p.~24]{Jin2026}}
For the equivariant family and normal weight lines of \cref{night:P3F.7,night:P3F.8}, use the Jin coordinates of \cref{night:P3F.3} and the retained sixfold parameter marking. The integer \(A=(4k-\ell)/24\) is independent of the equivariant normal trivialization and is additive under actual collar concatenation. Six parameter loops give six times the integer of one loop.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item Fix the orbit, Hopf and gluing conventions in P3F.7--8. For an orientation-preserving equivariant return preserving the two complex normal weight lines, its conifold replacement determines an integer

\[
A(\Phi)=\frac{4k(f)-\ell(f)}{24}.
\]

\item This integer is independent of the choice of equivariant tubular trivialization used for the replacement. It is additive under composition. In particular the actual return of the sixth parameter cover has integer exactly \(6A(\Phi)\). This assertion concerns the integral Torelli invariant; it does not infer a class in \(\mathbb Z/28\) from multiplication by \(6\) in \(\mathbb Z/28\).

\item Here is the complete framing comparison. After conjugating the negative normal line, the positive-weight bundle is \(E_+=\mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O(-1)\), trivial as an \(SU(2)\) bundle as in P3F.7. A loop of its unitary bundle automorphisms projectivizes to a loop of \(SO(3)\) gauge transformations of the normal quotient. To compare two replacement fillings, take the product of this loop with the collar of the boundary \(S^2\) and collapse its two ends. Its adjoint is a map

\[
\alpha:S^3\longrightarrow SO(3).
\]

\item On the replacement \(S^2\)-meridian times \(D^3\), this comparison is exactly \((x,y)\longmapsto(\alpha(y)x,y)\). This follows in each normal trivialization by applying the projectivized unitary matrix to the Hopf line \([u]\); on the common boundary the two original trivializations are those same matrices. Hence the comparison is the primitive-sphere twist \(a\) to an integral power, with no second Torelli component.

\item For precision about all loops, evaluation at one point gives the fibration \(\operatorname{Map}_*(S^2,SO(3))\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}(S^2,SO(3))\longrightarrow SO(3)\) with its constant-map section. Its fundamental group splits as \(\pi_3(SO(3))\oplus\pi_1(SO(3))\). The latter factor consists of matrices independent of the \(S^2\) variable and extends over \(D^3\); it contributes no boundary-clutching map. The first factor is exactly the displayed \(\alpha\). A loop of orientation-preserving parametrizations of the fixed \(S^2\) also extends by its radial \(SO(3)\) action on \(D^3\), after Smale1959 Theorem A (the strong deformation retraction of \(\operatorname{Diff}^+(S^2)\) to \(SO(3)\)); equivalently its only fundamental-group ambiguity is that same extending constant rotation. Thus it adds no second Torelli component. These statements describe the actual morphism from a normal-trivialization change to the return-map difference.

\item For the holomorphic phase loops the integer can be computed without any homotopy shorthand. Let \(n_-,n_+\) be their winding numbers on the original weight-minus and weight-plus lines. Over \(S^2_F\times S^2_\theta\), write \(h,t\) for the positive generators, and form the bundle obtained by clutching those phase loops. Its two positive-weight line classes are

\[
h-n_-t,\qquad -h+n_+t.
\]

\item Consequently \(c_1=(n_+-n_-)t\) and \(c_2=(n_-+n_+)ht\). The adjoint oriented three-plane bundle has

\[
p_1=c_1^2-4c_2=-4(n_-+n_+)ht.
\]

\item With Jin's generator \(\alpha\) normalized by \(p_1=+4\), the comparison is \(-(n_-+n_+)a\). In particular it can alter \(k\) and \(\ell\) by an arbitrary common multiple of \((1,4)\), but it leaves \(A\) unchanged. This fixes the sign of this phase-loop convention as well as its divisibility.

\item Jin Theorem 4.9, with \(g=1\), identifies the mapping-torus map with the homomorphism to Spin bordism over \(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}\); its characteristic coordinates are \((A,k)\). The representatives \(a,b\) have coordinates \(0,1\) and\(1,8\), respectively, as verified in P3F.3. For two returns choose tubular connections that are constant on a common collar and concatenate them. Their quotient replacements concatenate as the actual diffeomorphisms \(f\) and \(g\), so the replacement of the composite is \(fg\). Additivity of the cited bordism homomorphism gives \(A(fg)=A(f)+A(g)\). The framing calculation proves that this remains true for every separate choice of the tubular connections.

\item There is also a direct zero-class implication requiring no division in a finite group: the kernel of \(A\) in the exact presentation \(I(S^2\times S^3)=\mathbb Za\oplus\mathbb Zb\) is \(\mathbb Za\). P3F.4 constructs the Hopf lift of every \(a\)-power and extends it over \(D^4\times S^3\). Together with the pointwise cut-and-reglue identification P3F.8, it proves that the actual clutched sphere of a return in this kernel is standard. P3K.7--8 proves that the AC26 return belongs to this kernel, by two computations through the actual trace. The integral framework here then gives the reduction from six parameter loops to one.

\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{night:P3F.12}
\StatementRecord{night:P3F.12}{proved}{}{\SeriesRef{night:P2.2}}
Let \(C\) be the compact normalization of the actual component cover \(y^{12}=t^4/(t-1)^3\) in \SeriesRef{night:P2.2}, with its specified \(I_{12}\) extension and pulled-back point \(P\). The compact fixed-sheet torsor is smoothly translation-trivial through that model. Under the displayed translation isomorphism, its physical circle line differs from \(\mathcal O(P-O)\) by the pullback of a line on \(C\), hence by an integral fibre class in its first Chern class.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item The central-node component cover of the actual partial parameter filling is \(y^{12}=t^4/(t-1)^3\). Its compact normalization \(C\) has genus three, with one point above the cusp. The Jacobian after minimalization has one \(I_{12}\) fibre there. The affine defect of the actual fixed sheet around that point is translation by \(6P\): this is the first-coordinate part of \(\Delta_QF=\gamma-6\delta\) in P2.2, with \(q=Q^{12}\). We retain this defect in the following argument; the component cover alone did not remove it.

\item Let \(\Lambda_E\) be the source elliptic lattice on the complement of the cusp of \(C\). The original source matrices and cyclic-cover shifts are

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad\text{shift }4;\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\text{shift }-3.
\]

\item The commutator belongs to the cover subgroup, and

\[
G=[A,B]=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\quad
G-I=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad\det(G-I)=-1.
\]

\item Thus \(H_0(C\setminus\{\text{cusp}\};\Lambda_E)=0\) integrally. The exact calculation in \path{code/current_audits/audit_corrections/code/independent_IV_low_F_completion.py} multiplies the literal matrices \(ABA^{-1}B^{-1}\), verifies that their cyclic-cover character is zero, and obtains \(\det(G-I)=-1\). Thus \((G-I)\Lambda_E=\Lambda_E\), which already kills the full integral coinvariant group. Its output is \path{code/current_audits/audit_corrections/code/independent_IV_low_F_completion.json}. For \(C_0\) equal to \(C\) minus an open cusp disc, Poincare--Lefschetz duality with the oriented local system identifies \(H^2(C_0,\partial C_0;\Lambda_E)\) with this coinvariant group. The restriction \(H^1(C_0;\Lambda_E)\longrightarrow H^1(\partial C_0;\Lambda_E)\) is therefore surjective, including its torsion. Gluing the disc with the invariant-lattice extension \(j_*\Lambda_E\) gives \(H^2(C,j_*\Lambda_E)=0\). Equivalently, the top compact-support cohomology of the punctured curve is its integral coinvariant group; adding the skyscraper of local invariant sections changes no degree-two group.

\item The local sheaf here has a concrete meaning. On an \(I_n\) Tate chart with parameter \(Q\), the multiplicative parameter is \(Q^n\) times a unit. A translation in the identity component is multiplication of the Tate coordinate by a nonzero smooth unit \(a(Q)\). It acts in every resolved node chart by opposite unit multiplications; these formulas extend across all components of the \(I_n\) fibre. Locally \(a(Q)\) has a smooth logarithm. The kernel of this exponential consists of the invariant integral period: the other period contains \(\log Q\) and cannot be a smooth single-valued section through \(Q=0\). Hence, for the sheaf \(\mathcal A^0\) of these extending identity-component translations, there is an exact sequence

\[
0\longrightarrow j_*\Lambda_E\longrightarrow\mathcal L_\infty\longrightarrow\mathcal A^0\longrightarrow0,
\]

where \(\mathcal L_\infty\) is the sheaf of smooth sections of the extended complex Lie line bundle, and is fine. This verifies the sheaf at the singular fibre, rather than using the group law of the smooth fibres only. The local defect \(6P\) is in this identity component: \(P\) has a nonzero unit Tate coordinate at the original \(I_1\) fibre, and its pullback and all its multiples have component zero in \(I_{12}\). Its local logarithm therefore gives an extending translation.

\item It follows from the exact sequence and the vanishing just proved that \(H^1(C,\mathcal A^0)=0\). The actual affine fixed sheet, after the chosen local \(I_{12}\) extension, has a smooth translation section. Its translations extend through the fixed \(I_{12}\) resolution by the displayed unit formulas. It is therefore smoothly isomorphic, over \(C\) and by translations, to the sectioned Jacobian. This does not supply a holomorphic section or a holomorphic parameter filling.

\item The circle line also needs comparison under this isomorphism. Its fibrewise Picard point is \(P\), and its multidegree on the components of \(I_{12}\) is zero. The latter follows from the actual source line \(P-O\): both sections meet the identity component once, and neither meets any other component. The unit translation used above preserves the components and the fibrewise Picard point. Divide the transported line by \(\mathcal O(P'-O')\) on the Jacobian. On every smooth elliptic fibre this quotient is holomorphically trivial, and at \(I_{12}\) its unit gluing has product one and multidegree zero. Thus it is trivial on that fibre too.

\item Here is the local see-saw construction in this situation. Normalize a nonzero fibrewise holomorphic trivializing section at the zero section. Away from the nodal value it varies smoothly: it is the normalized one-dimensional kernel of the fibrewise Dolbeault operator. At \(I_{12}\) the construction uses the actual multiplicative unit charts: choose a frame on the first rational component and continue across the successive node units \(\eta_i\). The continued frame on the last component agrees with the first because \(\prod_i\eta_i=1\). The units and their logarithms extend smoothly in \(Q\), so this normalized frame extends over the nodal charts. Two such normalized local frames differ by a function of the base alone, because a holomorphic function on a connected compact fibre is constant. Their transition functions define a line bundle on \(C\). This proves, for the actual transported line, the equality

\[
c_1(L)=c_1\bigl(\mathcal O(P'-O')\bigr)+nF,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.
\]

\item It proves the required filtration statement via explicit normalized frames. In particular it does not infer that equality merely from triviality of the action on the associated graded of Leray. Since \(F^2=F\cdot(P'-O')=0\), its square is exactly \(-2\). The smooth affine comparison preserves orientation and signature, so \(p_1\) of the compact sheet pairs to \(-24\). The unspecified integer \(n\) records the permitted boundary gauge and has no effect on either of these pairings.

\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{night:P3F.13}
\StatementRecord{night:P3F.13}{proved}{}{\SeriesRef{night:P2.2}, \cref{iv:correction:P3K.6}, \cref{night:P3K.8}, \cref{night:P3K.9}}
\par\noindent\textit{Dependency scope.} We use \cref{iv:correction:P3K.6} only at their stated retained-construction or corrected-conclusion scopes.


The angular origin comparison is $\theta\gamma+6\theta(1-\theta)\delta$ and its full $Q$-deck line clutch has winding $-12$. The local corner charts below carry this clutch. Its monodromy application uses the real-trace, analytic-symbol and normal-framing maps of \cref{night:P3K.6,night:P3K.7,night:P3K.8,night:P3K.9}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item For the default twists let \(F(s,v)\) be the exact origin difference in P2.2, and keep \(\gamma(s,v)=(6\mu,C-s-12v)\). Direct polynomial subtraction gives, for real \(\theta\),

\[
F(s,v+\theta)-F(s,v)=\theta\gamma(s,v)+6\theta(1-\theta)\delta.\tag{P3F.13.1}
\]

\item On a fixed-radius parameter circle, \(v=ib+\theta\). The final summand is real in the \(\delta\) direction. It is a unitary gauge, equal to \(1\) after exponentiation at both endpoints. It can be removed by a homotopy of periodic gauges. The circle quotient of the origin comparison is therefore exactly the \(\gamma\)-translation loop, with all radial terms independent of \(\theta\).

\item The base deck must still be retained. Since \(\gamma(s+12,v)=\gamma(s,v)-12\delta\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
&[F(s+12,v+\theta)-F(s+12,v)]\\
&\qquad-[F(s,v+\theta)-F(s,v)]=-12\theta\delta.
\end{aligned}\tag{P3F.13.2}
\]

\item Thus the two angular lifts differ on the \(Q\)-deck by the unitary gauge \(\exp(-24\pi i\theta)\) in the \(\exp(2\pi i\zeta_2)\) convention, of winding \(-12\). This gauge is the integral clutch of the circle line. It does not disappear on passing to the orbit: its degree is retained by the principal circle bundle. The program \path{code/current_audits/audit_corrections/code/independent_IV_low_F_completion.py} subtracts the literal ordinary and cusp origins of \SeriesRef{night:P2.2}, checks both full differences and both endpoint values, and verifies the displayed small-resolution substitutions. The exact results are saved in \path{code/current_audits/audit_corrections/code/independent_IV_low_F_completion.json}.

\item The second Tate multiplier gives the normal-crossing chart \(XY=Qr\) after \(q=Q^{12}\), since \(q r^{12}=(Qr)^{12}\). Its elementary small resolution has charts

\[
X=Qz,\quad r=zY;\qquad Q=Xw,\quad Y=wr.
\]

\item At a node \(Q=uv\) of the resolved source \(I_{12}\) surface the remaining chart \(uv=Xw\) is resolved by

\[
X=uk,\quad v=kw;\qquad u=Xk,\quad w=kv.
\]

\item These four-variable charts are smooth and separate the central fixed surface from the fixed cusp trace. They give the local candidate for an orbit bordism after deleting fixed tubes. The central fixed-sheet normals have opposite weights and product trivial, so their positive Hopf projectivization is a product \(S^2\) bundle with Euler class \(u+c_1(L)\). This inner boundary is nonspin when the compact sheet has \(K=5F\). The canonical quotient structure is \(\mathrm{spin}^c\), with determinant class \(-K\) on that boundary; its nonzero second Stiefel--Whitney class is detected by the compact sheet\textquotesingle s section.

\item The displayed charts establish the local resolution and the exact clutch with its circle-line gauge. An outer-cusp identification requires a compatible morphism on the overlap; that morphism is not constructed by these local charts. The actual monodromy comparison uses the real trace of \cref{night:P3K.6,night:P3K.7}, the analytic-symbol map of \cref{night:P3K.8}, and the normal-framing map of \cref{night:P3K.9}. Their displayed maps retain this clutch and compute the original return.

\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{night:P3F.14}
\StatementRecord{night:P3F.14}{proved}{}{\cref{night:P3F.11}, \cref{night:P3F.12}, \cref{iv:correction:P3K.6}}
\par\noindent\textit{Dependency scope.} We use \cref{iv:correction:P3K.6} only at their stated retained-construction or corrected-conclusion scopes.


Let \(S\) be the compact complex fixed surface with normal lines \(L_+,L_-\) of circle weights \(+1,-1\), and put \(a=c_1(L_+)\), \(b=c_1(L_-)\), \(d=c_1(TS)\). For
\[
 \pi:B=\mathbb P(L_+\oplus\overline{L_-})\longrightarrow S,
\]
use the meridian-one hyperplane line \(U\), \(x=c_1(U)\), and the inherited spin\(^{c}\) determinant \(D=\pi^*(d+a+b)\). Its twisted index is
\[
 \int_B e^{D/2}e^x\widehat A(TB)=\chi(S,L_+).
\]
The physical-line application uses the extending map \(U=M^{-1}\) of \cref{night:P3K.68}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item This is the general calculation for the explicitly specified Hopf boundary. The earlier complex corner attempt did not supply a global boundary identification; the actual real trace P3K.6--9 now supplies the application and its complete orientation and line comparison. Let \(S\) be a compact complex surface, and let \(L_+,L_-\) be its two complex normal lines of circle weights \(+1,-1\) in a stable complex eight-dimensional chart. Write \(a=c_1(L_+)\), \(b=c_1(L_-)\), and \(d=c_1(TS)\).
Use the meridian-one hyperplane line \(U\) on the displayed Hopf
quotient, so \(x=c_1(U)\). The actual physical-line application
is transported through \(U=M^{-1}\) by \cref{night:P3K.68};
the zero calculation below is preserved by that explicit map. Its free normal-sphere quotient is \(B=\mathbb P(L_+\oplus\overline{L_-})\). Orient its sphere fibre so that the circle Euler class \(x\) has integral \(1\). Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_*(x)&=1,&\pi_*(x^2)&=a-b,\\
\pi_*(x^3)&=a^2-ab+b^2,&p_1(TB)&=\pi^*\bigl(p_1(TS)+(a+b)^2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

\item These follow from the projective-bundle relation with roots \(a,-b\). \begin{theorem}\label{night:P3F.24}
\StatementRecord{night:P3F.24}{proved}{}{Definitions and the displayed constructions; \cite[Section 3, p.~69]{Davis1982}}
Let \(\Phi\) be an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of the oriented six-sphere, with the boundary-identification convention in the proof. For the forward seam \((x,1)\sim(\Phi(x),0)\), the mapping torus is orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic to \((S^1\times S^6)\#\Sigma_\Phi\). Both spin structures have Eells--Kuiper invariant \(\mu(\Sigma_\Phi)\). A nonzero value excludes a diffeomorphism with the product in either orientation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item Let \(\Phi\) be an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of \(S^6\). Write \(\Sigma_\Phi=D^7\cup_\Phi(-D^7)\), with the direction of the boundary identification fixed from the first disc to the second. Its forward mapping torus satisfies \[
 T^+_\Phi=(S^6\times[0,1])/((z,1)\sim(\Phi(z),0))
       \cong(S^1\times S^6)\mathbin{\#}\Sigma_\Phi.   \tag{P3F.24.1}
\] Its reverse mapping torus, the convention used for the Jin six-dimensional mapping torus, satisfies \[
 T^-_\Phi=(S^6\times[0,1])/((z,0)\sim(\Phi(z),1))
       \cong(S^1\times S^6)\mathbin{\#}(-\Sigma_\Phi).\tag{P3F.24.2}
\] These are orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms for the indicated product and gluing orientations. For both spin structures on each mapping torus, its Eells--Kuiper invariant is respectively \(+\mu(\Sigma_\Phi)\) and \(-\mu(\Sigma_\Phi)\). In particular a nonzero such invariant excludes even an unoriented diffeomorphism with \(S^1\times S^6\).

\item \textbf{Proof.} First isotope \(\Phi\) to be the identity on a small oriented disc. The needed isotopy of disc embeddings is explicit: shrink the parametrized image disc toward its centre, move its centre along a path, move its oriented frame along the oriented frame bundle, and expand to the chosen target disc. Compactness gives a common sufficiently small radius along the path. Isotopy extension carries this isotopy to the ambient sphere. The result is a diffeomorphism equal to the identity on the target disc, and so supported in the complementary disc \(D^6\). Mapping tori of isotopic maps are diffeomorphic, by applying the isotopy along the interval; the same is true for their boundary-clutched spheres by extension over a collar. Thus this modification loses no data.

\item In the standard product \(S^1\times S^6\), choose a seam of the circle and the seven-ball \(B=D^6\times[-\epsilon,\epsilon]\) crossing that seam; round its corners. Its upper face has the positive orientation of \(D^6\), because the latter has even dimension. Define a boundary diffeomorphism of \(B\) to equal \(\Phi|_{D^6}\) on this face and the identity on the other face and the cylindrical collar. It is smooth since \(\Phi\) is the identity near \(\partial D^6\). Regluing this ball into its complement changes precisely the upper-to-lower seam identification to \(z\mapsto\Phi(z)\), and hence produces \(T^+_\Phi\). The boundary diffeomorphism, as an oriented map of \(\partial B\), is the original disc-supported \(\Phi\): both are its extension by the identity to the complementary six-disc.

\item The same regluing is connected sum with \(\Sigma_\Phi\). To check the map, remove an interior seven-ball from the second disc in \(D^7\cup_\Phi(-D^7)\). That remaining second piece is a collar \(S^6\times[0,1]\). Inserting this collar in the ball removed from \(S^1\times S^6\) gives exactly the specified boundary identification \(\Phi\). This proves (P3F.24.1) with its gluing direction. Replacing \(\Phi\) by \(\Phi^{-1}\) gives the reverse mapping torus and the reversed clutched sphere, proving \(P3F.24.2\).

\item There are exactly two spin structures because \(H^1(S^1\times S^6;\mathbb Z/2)=\mathbb Z/2\), and connected sum with a homotopy sphere does not change this group. Both product spin structures extend over \(S^1\times D^7\). That explicit eight-manifold has zero signature and zero first Pontryagin square. A homotopy seven-sphere bounds a spin eight-manifold; for instance the usual parallelizable representative supplied by \(\Theta _7=bP_8\) suffices. The boundary connected sum of this bounding manifold with \(S^1\times D^7\) bounds (P3F.24.1) for either spin structure. Its middle intersection form and its Pontryagin square are direct sums, since the joining handle has index one. Hence \[
 \mu(T^+_\Phi)=\mu(\Sigma_\Phi)
\] for each spin structure. The rational relative-to-absolute degree-four map is an isomorphism
because $H^3(T^+_\Phi;\mathbb Q)=H^4(T^+_\Phi;\mathbb Q)=0$.
For each chosen spin structure, we use the classical Eells--Kuiper
invariant in \cite[Section~1.4, equations~(2)--(3), p.~5 of
arXiv:1406.2226v3]{mapsCrowleyNordstrom19}. Its source normalization has
$p_W=p_1(W)/2$ and values in $\mathbb Q/28\mathbb Z$; division by $28$
gives exactly
\[
 \mu=\frac{p_1^2-4\sigma}{896}\pmod{\mathbb Z}
\]
in our convention. This cited invariant applies to closed spin
seven-manifolds with torsion $p_W|_{\partial W}$, and that class is zero
here. Orientation reversal changes its sign. Both values for the product are zero, so neither preserving nor reversing orientation can identify a nonzero example with that product.

\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}
